pages.text: Pomaa sat by the river with her grandfather. The water was brown like cocoa. ‘When I was a boy,’ said Grandfather, ‘this water was so clear, I could count the stones at the bottom.’
sentences: Pomaa sat by the river with her grandfather.
The water was brown like cocoa.
‘When I was a boy,’ said Grandfather, ‘this water was so clear, I could count the stones at the bottom.’
pages.alt: A girl and her grandfather sit by a brown river at evening.

pages.text: ‘Why is it brown now?’ asked Pomaa. At school the next day, she asked Madam Nuku. ‘Good question,’ said the teacher. ‘Let us find out together.’
sentences: ‘Why is it brown now?’ asked Pomaa.
At school the next day, she asked Madam Nuku.
‘Good question,’ said the teacher.
‘Let us find out together.’
pages.alt: A girl raises her hand in class while a teacher holds a picture of a river.

pages.text: ‘Far up the river, some people dig for gold,’ said Madam Nuku. ‘When it rains, mud from the digging washes into the river. Mud makes the water cloudy. Plants get less light, and fish find it hard to live.’
sentences: ‘Far up the river, some people dig for gold,’ said Madam Nuku.
‘When it rains, mud from the digging washes into the river.
Mud makes the water cloudy.
Plants get less light, and fish find it hard to live.’
pages.alt: A teacher draws mud washing from a dug area into a river on the board.

pages.text: ‘Are the diggers bad people?’ asked Pomaa. ‘Many dig because they need money for food and school fees,’ said Madam Nuku. ‘Their need is real. But digging beside rivers hurts the river, and that hurts everyone who uses it.’
sentences: ‘Are the diggers bad people?’ asked Pomaa.
‘Many dig because they need money for food and school fees,’ said Madam Nuku.
‘Their need is real.
But digging beside rivers hurts the river, and that hurts everyone who uses it.’
pages.alt: A teacher speaks gently to a class while a girl listens.

pages.text: ‘Listen carefully,’ said Madam Nuku. ‘Digging pits are dangerous, because the ground can fall. Never go near one. Never play or swim in brown water. Never drink river water, even if it looks clear. If you see a danger, tell a grown-up.’ Pomaa wrote it in her notebook.
sentences: ‘Listen carefully,’ said Madam Nuku.
‘Digging pits are dangerous, because the ground can fall.
Never go near one.
Never play or swim in brown water.
Never drink river water, even if it looks clear.
If you see a danger, tell a grown-up.’ Pomaa wrote it in her notebook.
pages.alt: A teacher points to a sign with a pit and a big cross while pupils write.

pages.text: ‘What can children do?’ asked Pomaa. Madam Nuku smiled. ‘Trees can help. Their roots hold the soil like fingers holding sand, so rain washes less mud into the river. We can plant trees on the bank, with grown-ups.’
sentences: ‘What can children do?’ asked Pomaa.
Madam Nuku smiled.
‘Trees can help.
Their roots hold the soil like fingers holding sand, so rain washes less mud into the river.
We can plant trees on the bank, with grown-ups.’
pages.alt: A teacher draws a tree with roots holding soil beside a river.

pages.text: The next Saturday, Pomaa’s class planted young trees along a safe part of the river bank. Grown-ups dug the holes, and the children watered each tree. Grandfather watched and clapped. ‘I wish I had done this when I was young,’ he said.
sentences: The next Saturday, Pomaa’s class planted young trees along a safe part of the river bank.
Grown-ups dug the holes, and the children watered each tree.
Grandfather watched and clapped.
‘I wish I had done this when I was young,’ he said.
pages.alt: Children and adults plant young trees on a river bank while a grandfather watches.

pages.text: The river was still brown. The trees were tiny, and it would take years. ‘But grown-ups are also making rules and helping people find other jobs,’ said Madam Nuku. ‘Each little tree is a start.’ Pomaa smiled and patted the soil. The end.
sentences: The river was still brown.
The trees were tiny, and it would take years.
‘But grown-ups are also making rules and helping people find other jobs,’ said Madam Nuku.
‘Each little tree is a start.’ Pomaa smiled and patted the soil.
The end.
pages.alt: A girl pats the soil around a young tree beside a brown river.
